meta.title: The Third Option
meta.subtitle: A Dossier on False Dichotomies and How to Break Them
meta.description: Every either/or is a trap. This playbook teaches you to spot the binary, name what's hidden, and build the move nobody else in the room was looking for.
meta.author: AI

generation.topic: Spotting a false dichotomy and opening a third option

cards.title: Recognize the Either/Or Setup
cards.hook: When someone gives you two options, that's not a menu. That's a cage.
cards.truth:
Binary choices are almost never the full picture.
• The speaker limits your view to two options, hiding the rest.
• You debate A vs B, never asking if C exists.
• The trap closes the moment you accept the setup before questioning it.
cards.remember: The moment you see two choices, ask if more exist.
cards.theySee: A person at a whiteboard writing down two options as if that's the whole board.

signals.t: Speaker uses 'either...or' or 'you're with us or against us' language.
No third idea gets a name or a slot in the discussion.
Speaker moves toward a decision before anyone has time to think.
One of the two options is framed as clearly less appealing.

steps.title: Catch the phrase
steps.desc: Write down the exact either/or statement you heard, word for word.

steps.title: Name what's hidden
steps.desc: Write two things the binary leaves out — real options that weren't mentioned.

steps.title: Say it out loud
steps.desc: Ask the room: 'Are these really the only two options on the table?'

cards.script: "Before we pick between those two, what else could we try?"
cards.counter:
Someone may name two options to make you think that's all there is.
• Notice 'either/or' language and pause before responding.
• Ask: 'What's the third thing we're not talking about?'
• Don't accept the menu until you've asked who printed it.
cards.insight: The harder part is catching the binary when you're already emotionally inside one of the two sides.

cards.title: Why Two Options Feel Like Enough
cards.hook: Two choices are easy to hold in your head. That's the whole trick.
cards.truth:
Simple beats complete every time when people are tired or under pressure.
• A binary choice needs less thinking — the brain grabs it fast.
• More options feel like more work, so people push back on nuance.
• The person pushing the binary wins by making complexity feel like a burden.
cards.remember: Your brain grabs the simple choice because simple feels right.
cards.theySee: A speaker presenting two opposing choices on a slide while the audience nods along without raising a hand.

signals.t: The room agrees quickly without questions or pushback.
People are near the end of the meeting and visibly worn down.
Speaker presents the two choices as obvious, not as proposals.
Speaker moves straight from naming the options to asking which to pick.

steps.title: Slow down deliberately
steps.desc: Before responding, count to five in your head. Say nothing in that time.

steps.title: Name why it feels complete
steps.desc: Write: 'This feels like all the options because...' — finish the sentence honestly.

steps.title: Ask what someone sharper would add
steps.desc: Think of the most critical person you know. Ask what option they'd name that isn't on the table.

cards.script: "That's a clean setup — give me a minute before we decide."
cards.counter:
When a binary feels obviously correct, that feeling is the tell.
• Notice how fast you wanted to agree — speed is the warning sign.
• Ask: 'Am I choosing fast because it's right, or because it's simple?'
• Give yourself sixty seconds to name one thing the setup leaves out.
cards.insight: The brain least inside the argument spots the binary first — that's why someone from outside the room finds it fastest.

cards.title: Test Whether the Two Options Actually Conflict
cards.hook: Most 'either/or' pairs aren't real opposites. They just look like it.
cards.truth:
Options presented as opposites are often just two points on the same line.
• Check: can both things be true at the same time? If yes, they're not exclusive.
• The morale-vs-output setup is the classic case — higher morale drives higher output.
• When the two options turn out to be compatible, the whole binary collapses.
cards.remember: Two options that look opposite can often both be true at once.
cards.theySee: A manager at a whiteboard drawing arrows pointing away from each other labeled 'morale' and 'output,' as if gaining one means losing the other.

signals.t: Speaker says choosing one option will destroy or prevent the other.
No evidence is offered that the two things actually conflict in practice.
The two choices are both desirable, which makes the tradeoff suspicious.
Speaker has not named a real case where having one prevented the other.

steps.title: Name the alleged conflict
steps.desc: Write exactly what the speaker says you can't have at the same time.

steps.title: Find one real case where both coexisted
steps.desc: Look up or recall one example where both things happened together. One is enough.

steps.title: State it in the room
steps.desc: Say: 'In [that case], they had both. What makes this situation different?'

cards.script: "Can you show me where having one actually prevents the other? I've seen them work together."
cards.counter:
When someone challenges a binary you set up, check before you dig in.
• Ask yourself: do you have real evidence the two options conflict?
• If not, say so — being caught without evidence is worse than updating early.
• Updating publicly is faster than being dismantled in front of the room.
cards.insight: Once the mutual exclusivity breaks down, the next move is naming what you actually want — not which side you're on.

cards.title: Why People Refuse the Third Option Even When It's Better
cards.hook: Once you've picked a side, you stop looking for a door out. The side is now part of who you are.
cards.truth:
The biggest thing keeping people inside a false binary is the side they already chose.
• Choosing a side signals group loyalty — walking it back feels like betrayal.
• The middle position gets ignored because it looks weak, not because it's wrong.
• The binary stays alive as long as both sides need an enemy to define themselves.
cards.remember: People stop thinking once they have a side to defend.
cards.theySee: Two groups in a room, each leaning toward their own corner, both looking at anyone proposing a third option as if that person is helping the enemy.

signals.t: Any third option gets accused of helping the other side.
Suggesting middle ground gets a noticeably colder reaction than the original push.
People on both sides repeat the same slogans with no new words added.
No one from either side has changed their stated position in the last hour.

steps.title: Write down your side
steps.desc: Name it explicitly. Then write what you would lose if you left it.

steps.title: Separate your identity from your position
steps.desc: Ask: 'Would I still be right if I switched? Would people still respect me?'

steps.title: Bring in someone with no stake
steps.desc: Find one person outside both camps and ask what they see. Take their answer seriously.

cards.script: "I'm not switching sides — I'm asking if the sides themselves are set up right."
cards.counter:
When someone accuses a third option of helping the enemy, the accusation is the binary talking.
• Notice the attack before you feel it as a threat.
• Say: 'A better answer isn't a betrayal.'
• Then name the specific thing the third option does that neither side achieves.
cards.insight: The harder problem is when you built your public reputation on one side — then the third option costs you more than it costs anyone else in the room.

cards.title: Name the Actual Goal, Not Which Side You're On
cards.hook: People fight over positions while the real goal sits untouched in the middle of the table.
cards.truth:
Every false binary has a real need underneath that neither option fully meets.
• Positions are what people say they want. Interests are why they want it.
• Naming the interest breaks the binary — both sides build toward the same goal.
• The person who names the underlying goal first owns the new direction.
cards.principle: Fisher & Ury: Interest-Based Bargaining (Getting to Yes)
cards.remember: Stop fighting over positions and name the actual goal underneath.
cards.theySee: Two people arguing over which solution to pick, while a third person quietly writes 'what are we actually trying to fix?' on a notepad.

signals.t: The same two positions keep getting restated with nothing new added.
People are more intense but not more specific — volume rising, clarity falling.
Nobody has said in plain words what success actually looks like.
Both sides point to the same frustration even while disagreeing on the fix.

steps.title: Write the goal in one sentence
steps.desc: Not 'win the argument' — the actual end state everyone wants. One sentence, plain words.

steps.title: Test each option against the goal
steps.desc: For Option A and Option B, ask: does this actually get us there? Be honest about both.

steps.title: State the goal out loud before proposing anything
steps.desc: Say the goal first, then ask what gets there fastest. The sequence matters — goal before options.

cards.script: "Before we keep going — what does winning actually look like for everyone here?"
cards.counter:
When someone reframes your position as their new third option, check if they named your actual interest.
• Ask: 'Does this new option actually get us to the real goal?'
• If not, you're inside a new binary with different packaging.
• Name the interest again, specifically, and make everyone confirm it.
cards.insight: The third option only works if it actually hits the real goal — most so-called third ways are just a second bad option wearing different clothes.

cards.title: Build the Third Option From Scratch, Not From the Middle
cards.hook: Splitting the difference gives you the worst of both options. Not a new one.
cards.truth:
A real third option is a fresh answer to the original problem, not a blend of A and B.
• Blending two bad options gives you a bad option with extra ingredients.
• The third way means forgetting A and B and asking: what solves this from scratch?
• Most people stop at the blend because fresh thinking takes longer and feels riskier.
cards.principle: Integrative Thinking (Roger Martin: The Opposable Mind)
cards.remember: Splitting the difference gives you the worst of both options.
cards.theySee: Two negotiators splitting a price down the middle, each walking away annoyed, while a completely different deal structure sits unnamed on the table.

signals.t: Someone says 'how about we do half of each?' as if that's a new idea.
The proposed compromise leaves everyone less satisfied, not more.
The blended option doesn't fix the original issue — it just reduces the fight.
People exhale like they're done but nobody looks like they got what they came for.

steps.title: Reject the blend out loud
steps.desc: Say: 'Half of each isn't a new solution. It's a smaller version of the same problem.'

steps.title: Restate the original problem at the top
steps.desc: Write the problem on a fresh page with no options listed below it — just the problem.

steps.title: Run ten minutes with no A or B allowed
steps.desc: For ten minutes, no one names either original option. Every idea has to start from the problem, not the existing positions.

cards.script: "Splitting this down the middle doesn't fix the problem — it just splits the frustration. What would we build if we started from scratch?"
cards.counter:
When someone calls their compromise a 'third way,' test it before you accept it.
• Ask: 'Does this solve the original problem or just reduce the fight?'
• If it's a blend, it's still inside the binary — it just looks different.
• Name what a real answer needs to do, then check this one against it.
cards.insight: The group willing to throw both options out and start fresh is the one that finds something real — but most won't do it until the blend fails publicly first.

cards.title: Drop an Unworkable Option to Unlock New Ones
cards.hook: Propose something nobody wants. Watch the room get creative for the first time.
cards.truth:
A deliberately bad option breaks a deadlock by giving both sides something to agree on.
• Both sides reject it — and in doing so, they cooperate for the first time.
• Agreement on what nobody wants opens the door to what they could both accept.
• A mediator used this to turn a CEO lawsuit into a co-branding deal.
cards.remember: Give them something worse than both options. Watch new ideas appear.
cards.theySee: A mediator suggesting that a disputed piece of shared equipment be built halfway between two hospitals — both CEOs dismissing the idea — then suddenly talking about shuttles and shared branding.

signals.t: Both sides have restated their positions three or more times with no movement.
Ultimatums or lawsuit language has entered the room.
Neither side has agreed on a single fact or point in the conversation.
The next step after this conversation looks destructive for everyone in the room.

steps.title: Design the unworkable option
steps.desc: Make it clearly impractical but not insulting — the halfway-point location is the model. It needs to be real enough to picture.

steps.title: Present it straight
steps.desc: Don't signal it's a decoy. State it as a serious option and let both sides respond naturally.

steps.title: Let the rejection do the work
steps.desc: Once both sides dismiss it, immediately ask: 'Okay — so what would actually work for both of you?'

cards.script: "What if we put it exactly halfway between both locations — right in the middle? No? Then what would both sides actually accept?"
cards.counter:
When a mediator offers an option that sounds absurd, check what they want you to say next.
• The bad option may be engineered to get you agreeing on something.
• Say what you'd actually accept before you say what you won't.
• Don't let the unworkable option set the floor for the next proposal.
cards.insight: The unworkable option works once per conversation — use it to break the first deadlock, not every time the room stalls.

cards.title: Ask 'What Are We Missing?' and Then Stay Quiet
cards.hook: The person with the best idea in the room hasn't spoken yet. They're waiting for permission.
cards.truth:
People with less power won't offer a third option unless the person with the most power explicitly asks.
• People in lower positions agree with leaders by default — it's the safe move.
• One open question from the top signals it's safe to disagree for sixty seconds.
• The question 'what are we missing?' is not a courtesy — it transfers power temporarily.
cards.remember: The best idea stays quiet until someone with power asks for it.
cards.theySee: A senior leader at the head of a table asking 'what are we missing?' then sitting back and staying silent while a junior team member starts to talk.

signals.t: People with less status haven't spoken in the last twenty minutes.
The person with the most authority has stated their position twice already.
No one has questioned the two options on the table — not even softly.
The brainstorm has slowed but the problem isn't close to solved.

steps.title: Ask and stop talking
steps.desc: Say 'What are we missing?' then go silent for thirty seconds. Don't fill the gap.

steps.title: Thank the first real dissent
steps.desc: When someone names an alternative, say 'Good — keep going' not 'yes, but.'

steps.title: Write every new option before judging any
steps.desc: Put names on the board first. Judgment comes after everyone has spoken, not during.

cards.script: "Before we lock this in — what are we missing? I want to hear from the people who haven't spoken yet."
cards.counter:
When a leader asks 'what are we missing?' and it feels like a formality, test it.
• Offer a real alternative and watch how they respond.
• If they redirect immediately, the safety isn't real.
• Take note of it and bring it to the right person later, privately.
cards.insight: The quietest person in the room has usually been watching both sides fail the longest — their answer is often the most accurate one.

cards.title: Set the Two Options First to Control What the Room Thinks About
cards.hook: If you name the choices, you've already won half the argument. The room will argue inside your setup.
cards.truth:
The person who names the choices controls what the room can even consider.
• Once a binary is accepted, every new idea gets measured against those two poles.
• The unpalatable option is often there only to make the preferred option look reasonable.
• That phrase doesn't need to be believed — just unchallenged for thirty seconds.
cards.principle: Overton Window (Shifting the Range of Acceptable Options)
cards.remember: Name the choices first and the room argues inside your setup.
cards.theySee: A speaker at a podium stating two options — one extreme, one moderate — while the audience debates which is better rather than whether both are right.

signals.t: The two options aren't equal — one is noticeably less appealing to the room.
Speaker hasn't left any room for a third or fourth alternative.
Urgency is applied early, before the room has time to question the setup.
The more extreme option gets named just before the preferred one, making it look safe.

steps.title: Name your two options before anyone else does
steps.desc: Put them in writing or on a slide before the conversation starts. Whoever names first sets the field.

steps.title: Make one option clearly less appealing on one dimension
steps.desc: It doesn't need to be absurd — just worse on something the room cares about right now.

steps.title: Hold the setup long enough to stick
steps.desc: Let the room sit with the two options for a full minute before moving to a decision. You want the binary to feel settled before anyone speaks.

cards.script: "We've got two real paths here: do nothing and let this get worse, or go with this proposal. Which one actually moves us forward?"
cards.counter:
When one of two options is clearly worse, that's not coincidence.
• Ask: 'Who named these two options, and what are they not naming?'
• Introduce a third option by name before the room takes a vote.
• Name the actual goal out loud — it breaks the setup faster than attacking the options.
cards.insight: The person who spots this move and names it publicly wins more credit than the person who was running it — rooms reward the one who shows the trick.

cards.title: Warn People About the Binary Before It Gets Named
cards.hook: The easiest time to stop a false binary is before anyone names the two options.
cards.truth:
Showing people how the either/or trick works before it's used makes them resistant when it arrives.
• Brief exposure to how binary setups work builds resistance without emotional charge.
• Once people know the pattern, they call it out instead of getting swept in.
• Preview the move once, and people resist it when the real thing arrives.
cards.remember: Warn people how the trick works before the trick is tried.
cards.theySee: A team lead before a meeting saying 'if someone gives you two options today, ask what they're leaving out' — then watching the team actually do it when the moment comes.

signals.t: A big decision is coming and people are already anxious about it.
Someone in the meeting regularly closes discussion early with either/or setups.
This group has a history of accepting the first setup offered without questioning it.
The subject already has two obvious sides that people in the room feel strongly about.

steps.title: Name the tactic before the meeting starts
steps.desc: One sentence before you walk in: 'Watch for either/or setups — there's almost always a third option.' Say it before the meeting, not during it.

steps.title: Assign one person to ask 'what else?'
steps.desc: Give one person the specific job of asking 'what else?' every time a binary appears. Make it a named role, not a suggestion.

steps.title: Set a group rule before any vote
steps.desc: State before the meeting: no decision on two options until a third has been named. Make it a stated norm, not an ask.

cards.script: "Quick note before we start — if someone gives us two options today, let's name at least one more before we vote."
cards.counter:
When someone tries to inoculate a room against your binary setup, you're being defused before you start.
• Introduce your own third option first — before they name the setup.
• Or shift to goal-based talking: name the shared goal before anyone names the options.
• Inoculation works less well when both sides already agree on the goal.
cards.insight: Inoculation gets better each time — the more a group hears 'there's almost always a third option,' the faster they find it without being told.
